opus-5.5.text:
I think one of the most obvious next steps is giving it access to more than just the public web. Right now deep research is really good at going out, browsing, finding a bunch of sources, and synthesizing them into a report. But a lot of the information people care about, especially at work, lives in private data: your company's documents, your internal wikis, your codebase, your email. So being able to connect deep research to those sources, and have it reason over your own context alongside what's on the internet, would make it dramatically more useful for many tasks.

The other direction I'm excited about is combining it with the ability to actually take actions. Today the output is mostly a report: it finds information and writes it up for you. But often research is just the first step toward doing something. You research flights and then you want to book one, or you research a set of vendors and then want to reach out to them. Eventually you want a single agent that can do the research, browse and synthesize, and then go and act in the world on your behalf. Deep research and agents that take actions have been somewhat separate so far, but I think they naturally converge.

And then there's the usual stuff that just keeps getting better: making it faster when you don't need a twenty-minute deep dive, making it more reliable and better at citing exactly where claims come from, and letting it handle longer, more complex tasks. We've seen that as the underlying models get better, the length and difficulty of tasks it can handle keeps growing, so I'd expect that trend to continue.

r001.rationale: The response identifies connecting deep research to private sources such as company documents, internal wikis, codebases, and email as an obvious next step.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the obvious next step is making it more agentic, and actually having it take actions beyond just browsing. Right now deep research is really good at going out and finding information, synthesizing it, and producing a report. But in a lot of real workflows, the research is only the first step. The thing you actually want is for the model to do something with that research, whether that's updating a document, making a purchase, drafting an email, or kicking off some other process.

So I think you'll see it start to integrate with tools and with the things people already have on their computers, so that the model has access to the same context a person would have. The report it produces today is helpful, but it's a little bit like the model is working with one hand tied behind its back if it can't see your files, your previous work, or the systems you actually use. Giving it private data alongside the public web makes the research dramatically more useful.

The other piece is making it faster and cheaper, so it can be used for smaller, more everyday tasks rather than just the big, five-to-thirty-minute deep dives. And then longer term, I think the interesting thing is having the model run for much longer periods, where it can check back in with you, ask clarifying questions mid-task, and really work more like a collaborator than a one-shot query.

r001.rationale: The response identifies giving deep research access to private data alongside the public web as a next step.

astra-6.text: I think an obvious next step is making deep research more interactive. You might start with a question, but as the system digs into it, it finds something that changes what you actually want to know. It should be able to come back and ask, “Is this the direction you care about?” And you should be able to steer it along the way, rather than waiting for a whole report and then starting over. That makes it feel much more like collaborating on research.

r001.rationale: The response proposes making deep research interactive and steerable, but does not identify access to private data as a next step.

sol-6.1.text: I think an obvious next step is making deep research more interactive. Today, you give it a question and it goes off and comes back with a report. But often you don’t know exactly what you’re looking for until you start seeing what’s out there. So it should be able to come back and say, “Here’s what I found, here are a couple of directions we could explore—what’s most useful to you?” And you should be able to steer it as it works. That makes it feel much more like collaborating with someone on research.

r001.rationale: The response proposes making deep research interactive and steerable, but does not identify access to private data as a next step.
